claims.text: The catalyst consists of platinum-group metals configured as 1D hierarchical Pt-alloy nanostructures.
The catalyst has a well-defined morphology and alloy composition.
The 1D hierarchical architecture increases active surface area and active-site accessibility.
The 1D hierarchical architecture improves reactant delivery and product removal through enhanced mass transport.
Alloying modifies the Pt electronic structure and shifts its d-band center.
The alloy-induced electronic modification tunes the adsorption energies of ethanol and its reaction intermediates.
The combined architectural and alloying effects stabilize key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The combined architectural and alloying effects lower ethanol-oxidation activation barriers.
The combined architectural and alloying effects prevent catalyst-surface poisoning.
Enhanced surface accessibility, mass transport, and alloy-modified adsorption jointly govern the catalyst's ethanol-oxidation activity, selectivity, and durability.
Disrupting the hierarchical nanostructure will reduce catalytic current density relative to the intact catalyst.
Disrupting the hierarchical nanostructure will diminish selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Disrupting the hierarchical nanostructure will accelerate performance degradation.
Removing or varying the secondary alloying element will reduce catalytic current density relative to the intact alloy.
Removing or varying the secondary alloying element will diminish selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Removing or varying the secondary alloying element will accelerate performance degradation.
A 12-electron ethanol-oxidation mechanism is expected under the specified acidic operating potentials.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies under moderate acidity and temperature and may fail at extreme temperature or pH or in non-alcohol oxidation.
Different deactivation pathways or mass-transport limitations can dominate outside the proposed reaction regime.
